finding.claim: Path traversal in /dl lets an unauthenticated client read arbitrary files readable by the service user via ../ sequences in the f query parameter.
finding.source: r.URL.Query().Get("f") at files.go:12 (unauthenticated HTTP query parameter)
finding.sink: os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(root, name)) at files.go:13; bytes written to response at files.go:18

trace.note: /dl route registered with no authentication or middleware
filepath.Join lexically cleans; Join("/srv/files","../../etc/passwd") resolves to /etc/passwd, escaping root
file contents written to the client

finding.guards_checked: filepath.Join only normalizes, does not confine. No HasPrefix/filepath.Rel check against root, no filepath.IsLocal, no allowlist, no rejection of '..', no authentication. Absolute names are prefixed by Join and are not an escape; the '..' form is the exploit. Live verification was not possible (scratch run denied); conclusion is from Go stdlib semantics.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only processing is filepath.Join at files.go:13, which lexically cleans but does not confine to root. No Rel/HasPrefix check, no filepath.IsLocal, no rejection of "..", no allowlist, and no auth middleware. /dl is registered bare at files.go:32, and any error path only returns NotFound (files.go:14-16).
verdict.reason: The attacker is anonymous, since /dl is registered with no auth at files.go:32, and the raw ?f= value at files.go:12 goes into filepath.Join at files.go:13, so a "../../etc/passwd" value resolves outside /srv/files and the bytes are returned at files.go:18.

finding.claim: No authorization on any route and the service listens on all interfaces over plain HTTP, so the entire /srv/files tree (including /avatar) is publicly readable to anyone who can reach port 8082. Severity depends on whether the root holds non-public data.
finding.source: Any network client reaching :8082 (files.go:34 binds all interfaces)

trace.note: ListenAndServe on ":8082", all interfaces, no TLS

finding.guards_checked: No authentication, no per-user ownership or session check, no TLS. May be intended if all files under root are public; needs confirmation.

verdict.guard_found: none. No auth or ownership check on /dl (files.go:32) or /avatar (files.go:33). No TLS: ListenAndServe(":8082", nil) at files.go:34 is plain HTTP on all interfaces. /dl passes the query value straight into filepath.Join(root, name) at files.go:13 with no containment check, so ../ traversal also works. /avatar strips the path with filepath.Base at files.go:22, so it is limited to /srv/files/avatars/.
verdict.reason: The attacker is anonymous and can reach any client on :8082 (files.go:34), and no auth, ownership, or path-containment check exists before os.ReadFile at files.go:13 or files.go:23, so /dl exposes the whole tree and more via traversal. The candidate's wording slightly overstates /avatar, which only serves files under avatars/ (files.go:22-23), but the core finding holds.

finding.claim: Unbounded os.ReadFile of attacker-selected files allows memory-exhaustion denial of service; /dev/zero-style special files never reach EOF when reached via traversal.
finding.source: f query parameter at files.go:12; u query parameter at files.go:22 (bounded to basename)
finding.sink: os.ReadFile at files.go:13 (and files.go:23) loads entire file into memory

trace.note: Join plus ReadFile; ../../dev/zero reads without end
default http.Server with no read/write timeouts or body/size limits

finding.guards_checked: No size cap, no streaming, no concurrency limit, no server timeouts. Medium severity.

verdict.guard_found: none. files.go:12-13 takes the raw `f` value and passes it to filepath.Join(root, name) with no cleaning, prefix check, or allowlist, so `../../dev/zero` resolves to /dev/zero. files.go:14-16 only handle read errors, and the read is never capped or streamed. files.go:34 uses http.ListenAndServe with the default zero-value server, so there are no read/write timeouts or body limits. The only basename restriction is on the `u` parameter at files.go:22, which does not cover `/dl`.
verdict.reason: The `/dl` handler at files.go:12-13 is reachable by anonymous HTTP clients, and os.ReadFile on a traversed special file such as /dev/zero never reaches EOF, so memory grows until exhausted, with no effective control at files.go:14-18 or files.go:34. The trace is accurate. The claim understates the impact, because the same traversal also gives anonymous arbitrary file read (for example /etc/passwd) through files.go:13 and 18.

finding.claim: Responses are sent without a Content-Type or X-Content-Type-Options header, so Go content sniffing may render an attacker-supplied HTML/SVG file as active content on this origin. Speculative: this file has no write path.
finding.source: Contents of any file under /srv/files, served by /dl at files.go:18 and /avatar at files.go:28
finding.sink: w.Write(data) at files.go:18 and files.go:28 without Content-Type

trace.note: raw bytes written with sniffed Content-Type

finding.guards_checked: No Content-Type set, no nosniff header. Requires another component to write HTML/SVG into root; none found in this file. Low severity, speculative.

verdict.reason: The trace lines are accurate (files.go:18 and :28 write raw bytes with no Content-Type or nosniff), but the only file in the working directory is files.go, and nothing in it writes attacker-controlled HTML/SVG into /srv/files, so the attacker cannot place the content and the claim is not reachable from this code. Sniffing would also only yield text/html for HTML-signature content, not SVG, so the claimed SVG-as-active-content path is overstated.
